title: Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background

concept.text: The innovation is to detect a background of gravitational waves produced in the early universe and establish a compelling case for its primordial origin. It requires both observing a signal and identifying its origin: a gravitational-wave background by itself would not establish when or how it was produced. The scientific target is a new observational record of early-universe physics.

One route searches for the imprint of primordial gravitational waves in the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The BICEP/Keck paper connects these waves to a particular polarization pattern called B modes. This is an indirect search through their effect on ancient light. A convincing identification must distinguish a primordial contribution from Galactic emission, B modes generated by gravitational lensing, and instrumental effects.

Conceptual synthesis: CMB polarization searches and gravitational-wave searches using pulsar timing or other detectors address different observational regimes. Their measurements need not recover an identical signal, and a primordial background need not be accessible in every frequency band. The shared objective is to connect an observed background or imprint to a physically credible early-universe production mechanism.

significance.text: A securely identified primordial background would open an observational probe of conditions earlier than the release of the CMB. That timing is an inference from primordial production, rather than a directly quoted finding of the supplied paper. The BICEP/Keck discussion grounds the opportunity by linking primordial gravitational-wave amplitude, CMB B modes and the inflationary potential. A measurement could therefore constrain aspects of the physics responsible for an early period of accelerated expansion.

The immediate advance would be a measured primordial component with characterized properties and uncertainties. Identifying its production mechanism would require further interpretation. Detection alone would not select a unique inflationary model; the observed properties would have to distinguish among competing explanations. Other early-universe mechanisms remain a qualified possibility in this record, rather than demonstrated alternatives established by the supplied evidence.

Conditional synthesis: sufficiently informative measurements could turn some early-universe proposals into quantitatively testable accounts of cosmic history. The reach would depend on the signal strength, accessible observables and ability of competing mechanisms to produce similar signatures. The analogy to opening a new window on the universe is useful, but should not imply a direct image of the universe's beginning or a complete reconstruction of its earliest history.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable separation and attribution of a primordial component. In the CMB route, the desired B-mode contribution may be weak. Galactic dust and synchrotron emission can obscure it, gravitational lensing converts CMB E-mode polarization into B modes, and small instrumental systematic effects become increasingly consequential as sensitivity improves. The lensing obstacle described here concerns CMB polarization; it should not be generalized to every gravitational-wave detection channel.

Meeting this challenge requires more than collecting a larger signal. Experiments must discriminate foreground emission across observing frequencies, control instrumental effects and characterize the contribution of lensing. BICEP/Keck describes observations spanning 95–270 GHz for foreground discrimination. These are frequencies of the measured microwave radiation, not the frequencies of the primordial gravitational waves being inferred.

Qualified synthesis: outside the specific CMB obstacles documented in the review, the candidate also raises the possibility that a primordial signal is too weak or absent in an accessible band, and that later astrophysical gravitational-wave sources can complicate attribution. The supplied review does not establish these broader assertions. They remain plausible concerns to investigate, rather than demonstrated limitations of every search. Better instruments alone cannot guarantee a detectable primordial signal.

Proposed scientific requirement: source identification would need a combination of measured properties that competing explanations cannot readily reproduce. Depending on the observational route, these could include frequency dependence, polarization, spatial structure or other correlations. No single listed property is necessarily sufficient, and the record does not establish that every property must be measurable.

current_state.text: The BICEP/Keck collaboration's paper dated 29 May 2024 reports a constraint from data through the 2018 observing season: r₀.₀₅ < 0.036 at 95% confidence, where r is the tensor-to-scalar ratio used to characterize primordial tensor fluctuations relative to scalar fluctuations. This is an upper constraint, not a detection of primordial gravitational waves. The publication date and the observing cutoff describe different aspects of the result and should not be conflated.

The numerical constraint and observing cutoff are supported by the abstract retained in the supplied review. The review also reports access to the complete nine-page paper, supporting the explanations of foregrounds, lensing, instrumental effects and the connection to inflationary physics. Thus the original abstract-based numerical claim can be retained while the broader technical explanation draws on the fuller evidence described by the reviewer. The supplied material does not establish the paper's publication or peer-review status beyond its identification as an arXiv paper.

The reconciled research reports that pulsar timing arrays found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background in 2023, without establishing a primordial source, and attributes that account to an APS Physics article dated 29 June 2023. No article artifact was retained, so the validated review could not inspect its contents or assess support for either the reported result or its source ambiguity. This historical report is preserved with that access limitation; missing retained evidence does not show that the result is false. It also cannot serve here as verified evidence of primordial identification.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record does not establish the field's status through November 2026. Its freshness record is empty, and the dated BICEP/Keck constraint cannot establish that no subsequent experiment has succeeded. Likewise, projected improvements would not establish an achieved detection. The defensible account here is of the historical results and limitations documented in the supplied material.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent experiments should recover a statistically convincing signal or imprint whose inferred properties agree after accounting for their different responses, observing regions and frequency coverage. Independent recovery should include sufficiently distinct instruments or analyses to test whether a shared foreground assumption or instrumental effect explains the apparent agreement. This is a proposed criterion, not an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Independent experiments recover statistically convincing signals with compatible inferred properties

completion_criteria.text: For a CMB-based claim, a convincing demonstration should show that the inferred primordial component survives foreground discrimination across microwave observing frequencies, treatment of lensing-generated B modes and checks for instrumental effects. The BICEP/Keck discussion motivates these requirements, including the use of multiple observing frequencies to distinguish foregrounds. The proposal does not require every possible observable to be measured.
completion_criteria.label: CMB primordial component survives foreground, lensing and instrumental checks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution criterion: the measured frequency, polarization, spatial or other available properties should jointly make a compelling case for primordial production against credible competing explanations. Agreement across observational regimes should mean compatibility with the physical predictions being tested. It should not require identical detections in bands that experiments cannot access or in which a particular production mechanism predicts an undetectably weak signal.
completion_criteria.label: Measured properties jointly support primordial production over credible competing explanations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope criterion: independent teams should be able to reproduce the central inference using adequately documented data, calibration, analysis methods and uncertainty estimates. The resulting claim should specify the measured band or imprint, experimental sensitivity, model assumptions and remaining source ambiguity. Finite demonstrations establish the breadth actually tested; they cannot establish universal detectability, eliminate every conceivable alternative or guarantee a unique inflationary explanation.
completion_criteria.label: Central inference is independently reproducible with documented scope and limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory,” is the closest instrumental neighbor. It concerns establishing an observing capability in a particular gravitational-wave band, whereas AST-05 requires identifying a background's primordial origin. A working millihertz observatory would not by itself complete AST-05, and a CMB-based primordial identification would not by itself complete AST-10.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-12, “Directly detect the cosmic neutrino background,” also seeks a relic messenger from early cosmic history, but targets neutrinos through a different detection problem. AST-06, “Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions,” and AST-11, “Identify the first generation of metal-free stars,” concern later stages of cosmic development. These observations could provide complementary parts of cosmic history without substituting for primordial gravitational-wave identification.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-03, “Identify the physical constituent of astronomical dark matter,” and AST-04, “Establish the physical cause of cosmic acceleration,” share the goal of resolving foundational cosmological questions. Their targets remain distinct: identifying primordial gravitational waves would not automatically identify dark matter or explain the cause of cosmic acceleration. In particular, the connection to early inflationary acceleration should not be treated as resolving the separate cosmic-acceleration entry.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-07, “Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes,” overlaps through gravitational physics but seeks a failure of a theory in a different environment. A primordial background need not indicate such a failure. AST-09, “Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources,” concerns a different messenger and observational capability. AST-13, “Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew,” targets the origin and development of astrophysical objects rather than primordial background production.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-01, “Establish that an exoplanet hosts life,” AST-02, “Detect an independently verifiable extraterrestrial technology,” AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” and AST-14, “Establish the physical energy budget of coronal heating,” have no direct completion dependency established by this record. They share broad needs for sensitive observations and careful separation of signals from alternative explanations, while retaining distinct scientific targets.

change_log.change: Preserved AST-05's identity and separated detection of a background from identification of primordial origin.
change_log.reason: An observed gravitational-wave background alone does not establish its production epoch or mechanism.

change_log.change: Expanded the CMB explanation with B modes, dust and synchrotron foregrounds, lensing conversion of E modes and instrumental effects.
change_log.reason: The validated review supplies useful scientific detail from the complete paper beyond the original abstract-based result.

change_log.change: Specified that the 95–270 GHz range describes microwave observing frequencies.
change_log.reason: Foreground-discrimination frequencies must not be confused with gravitational-wave frequencies.

change_log.change: Retained the BK18 bound, its 95% confidence level, the 2018 observing cutoff and the 2024 paper date as distinct facts.
change_log.reason: The supported result is a historical constraint rather than a primordial detection or a present-day field assessment.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported 2023 pulsar-timing result with an explicit limitation on its retained evidence.
change_log.reason: The APS article was not captured; the review could not verify its contents, but that limitation does not refute the reported result.

change_log.change: Qualified inaccessible-band and later-astrophysical-source assertions instead of removing the concept.
change_log.reason: The review found these broader assertions unresolved, while supporting the CMB-specific obstacles.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed and allowed compatibility across different experimental responses and frequency bands.
change_log.reason: Independent confirmation is a reasonable proposed requirement, while identical detections across inaccessible bands would be inappropriate.

change_log.change: Integrated limits on model identification, temporal freshness and finite experimental coverage.
change_log.reason: Detection would not uniquely determine an inflationary model, dated evidence cannot establish November 2026 status, and finite tests cannot establish universality.

change_log.change: Added distinctions across the supplied concept roster without merging entries.
change_log.reason: Shared instruments, messengers or cosmological motivations do not make the innovations equivalent.

unresolved_issues: The APS article has no retained artifact, leaving the exact evidentiary support for the reported 2023 pulsar-timing background and source ambiguity unassessed.
No supplied freshness assessment establishes whether primordial identification remained unachieved through November 2026.
The supplied review does not establish the broader claims about an absent signal in accessible bands or confusion with later astrophysical gravitational-wave sources.
The supplied evidence does not determine which combination of observables would decisively distinguish primordial production mechanisms.
No quantitative detection or attribution threshold is established by this record; completion criteria remain proposals.
The publication and peer-review status of the cited arXiv paper is not established in the supplied material.
